questions.q: What was the immediate trigger for the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and which treaty did it revise?
questions.a: The immediate trigger was the Russo-Turkish War (1877–78), which ended with the Treaty of San Stefano (March 1878) creating a large Russian-influenced Bulgaria. The Congress of Berlin (June–July 1878), called by Bismarck, revised San Stefano to reduce Bulgarian territory and limit Russian influence. A wrong answer — such as naming the Treaty of Versailles or the Crimean War — reveals the student confuses the sequence of 19th-century diplomatic congresses and cannot distinguish the "Eastern Question" crises from later settlements.

questions.q: Why did Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1908 provoke a major international crisis, even though it had administered the provinces since 1878?
questions.a: Administration (occupation) under the Congress of Berlin was temporary and nominally under Ottoman sovereignty; annexation in 1908 unilaterally ended Ottoman suzerainty, violated the Treaty of Berlin, and threatened the balance of power by strengthening Austria-Hungary in the Balkans. It enraged Serbia (which wanted Bosnia for a South Slav state) and humiliated Russia (which had backed down without gains). A wrong answer that treats occupation and annexation as the same thing shows the student misses the legal-diplomatic distinction that made 1908 a crisis point — a classic board exam trap.

questions.q: A historian argues: "The Balkan Wars (1912–13) were a rehearsal for World War I." Using two specific pieces of evidence, evaluate this claim.
questions.a: Evidence supporting the claim: (1) The Balkan League (Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, Montenegro) formed under Russian encouragement mirrored the alliance systems of 1914; (2) The wars saw modern weaponry, trench warfare, and civilian targeting that foreshadowed WWI tactics. Evidence complicating the claim: The Balkan Wars were regional conflicts over Ottoman territory, not a general European war — the great powers (except Austria-Hungary) largely stayed out militarily. A student who only lists similarities without noting the limited great-power involvement shows an inability to evaluate historical analogies critically — a key competency skill.

questions.q: Compare the nationalist goals of Serbia and Bulgaria in the period 1878–1914. How did their differing visions of a "South Slav" future contribute to the Second Balkan War (1913)?
questions.a: Serbia sought a Greater Serbia/Yugoslavia incorporating Bosnia, Macedonia, and Kosovo — an outlet to the Adriatic. Bulgaria aimed for a Greater Bulgaria based on San Stefano boundaries, claiming Macedonia as ethnically Bulgarian. Both claimed Macedonia; when the First Balkan War expelled the Ottomans, they fought each other (Second Balkan War, 1913) over the spoils. Bulgaria attacked its former allies, was defeated, and lost territory. A wrong answer that treats all Balkan nationalisms as identical misses the irreducible territorial conflicts that prevented a unified South Slav front — a crucial analytical distinction for board exams.

questions.q: "Gavrilo Princip was a pawn of Serbian military intelligence (the Black Hand), not a genuine nationalist." Assess this interpretation using the concept of state-sponsored terrorism vs. revolutionary nationalism.
questions.a: Princip was a member of Young Bosnia, a revolutionary nationalist group inspired by Serbian irredentism but not directly controlled by the Serbian government. The Black Hand (led by Colonel Apis) provided weapons and training, but the Serbian government (Prime Minister Pašić) knew of the plot and tried weakly to stop it. The assassination blended genuine nationalist motivation with state-tolerated covert action. A student who calls Princip either a "pure patriot" or a "mere puppet" fails to grasp the blurred line between revolutionary movements and state policy — a nuance examiners reward in source-based questions.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (1875–1914) showing how each crisis in the Balkans altered the alliance system of Europe. Annotate each entry with the specific shift in great power relations.
questions.a: Expected entries: 1875 Herzegovina Uprising → 1878 Congress of Berlin (Three Emperors League strained, Austria-Russia rivalry sharpens) → 1879 Dual Alliance (Germany-Austria) → 1881 Three Emperors League renewed (fragile) → 1887 Reinsurance Treaty (Germany-Russia, lapses 1890) → 1908 Bosnian Crisis (Russia humiliated, turns to France/Britain) → 1912–13 Balkan Wars (Austria determined to crush Serbia, Germany gives "blank cheque" assurance) → 1914 Sarajevo. A poor timeline lists events without annotating alliance shifts, showing the student sees crises as isolated episodes rather than a cascade restructuring European diplomacy.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Balkans Crisis (1870s–1914) refers to the series of ______ uprisings, great power rivalries, and diplomatic conflicts in the Balkan Peninsula (Southeast Europe) where subject peoples of the declining Ottoman Empire — Serbs, Greeks, Bulgarians, Romanians, Albanians — demanded nation-states based on ethnic identity, while Austria-Hungary, Russia, Britain, France, and Germany competed to control the strategic region, ultimately making it the "powder keg" that ignited World War I.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are standing at the Latin Bridge in Sarajevo — the very spot where a 19-year-old Serbian ______, Gavrilo Princip, fired the shots that started World War I.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are standing at the Latin Bridge in Sarajevo — the very spot where a ______-year-old Serbian nationalist, Gavrilo Princip, fired the shots that started World War I.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain how the intersection of ethnic nationalism and imperial rivalry in the Balkans created a chain of crises (1875–1914) that destabilized the European balance of power, and can trace the specific causal links from the Congress of Berlin (1878) through the Balkan Wars (1912–13) to the assassination at Sarajevo (1914).
